title: Typed Functions
subtitle: Parameter types, return types, optional params, overloads, and function types
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: In JavaScript, functions are one of the most common sources of type bugs — passing the wrong argument type, ignoring the return value, or calling a function with the wrong number of arguments.
whyItExists.solution: TypeScript enforces parameter types and return types at every call site. Optional and default parameters are typed explicitly. Function types describe the shape of callbacks and higher-order functions.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Always type function parameters. Let TypeScript infer the return type unless being explicit adds documentation value or prevents accidental widening.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Avoid over-specifying the return type for simple functions where inference is obvious. Don't use overloads when a union type would do — overloads are for complex type relationships.

explainModes.beginner: When you write a function in TypeScript, you label each parameter with its type and say what the function returns. TypeScript then checks every place you call the function — wrong number of arguments, wrong type, ignoring a required value — and shows an error immediately.
explainModes.simple: function f(a: number, b: string): boolean. Optional parameter: b?: string (type is string | undefined). Default parameter: b = 'hello' (type inferred). Rest parameter: ...args: number[]. Callback type: (n: number) => string. Function type alias: type Transform = (input: string) => string. Arrow function: const double = (n: number): number => n * 2.
explainModes.standard: void vs undefined: void means 'caller shouldn't use the return value'; undefined means the value is literally undefined. A function typed as () => void can return a value from an implementation perspective (TS allows it) but callers can't use it. this parameter: function greet(this: User, greeting: string) — explicitly types this inside a function. Parameter destructuring with types: function f({ name, age }: { name: string; age: number }). Readonly parameters: function f(readonly arr: number[]) — prevents mutation.
explainModes.technical: Overloads: multiple signatures + one implementation signature. The implementation signature is private — callers only see the overload signatures. TypeScript resolves overloads top-to-bottom. Callback compatibility: (err: Error, data: string) => void is compatible with () => void (extra params are ignored). This is why .forEach's callback can have 1, 2, or 3 params. Generic functions: function identity<T>(arg: T): T — covered in generics lesson.
explainModes.deepDive: Function type compatibility is contravariant for parameters and covariant for return types. This matters for callback types: a function that handles fewer params is assignable to a type that handles more. Conditional types on function overloads: TypeScript picks the first matching overload, not the union of all. Async functions: async function f(): Promise<string> — return type is always Promise<T>. The await keyword strips the Promise. Top-level await is available in ES2022+ modules.

questions.question: What is the type of parameter `b` in `function f(a: string, b?: number): void`?
questions.explanation: Optional parameters (marked with ?) have type T | undefined. When the caller omits b, TypeScript treats its value as undefined inside the function. This is why you must check if (b !== undefined) before using b as a number.

faq.q: When should I annotate the return type vs let TypeScript infer it?
faq.a: Let TypeScript infer for short, simple functions. Annotate explicitly when: the function is exported (public API), the inferred return type is wider than intended, or the function body is complex enough that a wrong return could be missed. For async functions, always annotate Promise<T> — it documents the resolved type clearly.

examples: type EventHandler<E extends Event> = (e: E) => void
function debounce<T extends (...args: any[]) => void>(fn: T, ms: number): T
async function getUser(id: number): Promise<User | null>
